lesson.title: Many Genes, One Trait: The Continuous Spectrum of Height
lesson.summary: Traits shaped by many genes acting together, rather than one gene with a couple of clear cut dominant and recessive forms, produce a smooth continuum of phenotypes instead of a few discrete categories.
lesson.body:
Every trait examined so far, seed shape, flower color, blood type, is controlled by a single gene, which is exactly why each one sorts cleanly into a handful of distinct phenotype categories. Many real traits do not behave that way. A polygenic trait is shaped by several different genes acting at the same time, with each gene contributing a small additive push to the overall phenotype rather than a single gene calling all the shots.

Human height is a well studied polygenic trait. A large number of genes are each known to nudge height up or down by a small amount, and the combined additive effect of all of them, layered on top of environmental factors such as childhood nutrition, produces the smooth, bell shaped distribution of adult heights seen across a population, rather than a few sharply separated height classes. Human skin color and eye color are shaped by multiple genes acting together as well, though exactly how many genes are involved and how they interact is still an active area of research, and the classic simplified teaching models of these traits capture only part of the real underlying complexity.

The reason more genes produce smoother variation follows directly from the math already built up in earlier chapters. A single gene with two alleles, crossed as Aa by Aa, produces at most three genotype classes. Add a second independent gene, as in a dihybrid cross, and the number of genotype and phenotype combinations multiplies. Add many genes at once, each contributing its own small effect, and the number of possible combinations grows so large that the discrete categories blur together into what looks like continuous variation, a smooth curve rather than a bar chart with only a few bars.

The connection between genotype and phenotype still holds for polygenic traits. Phenotype is still the product of the underlying genotypes at every contributing gene, combined with environmental input, it is simply much harder to work backward from a measured height to the exact combination of alleles that produced it, because so many different genotype combinations can add up to the very same phenotype.
